name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm field manager at Marsh End, about 250 hectares of carrots, leeks and cabbages that go to two supermarkets. I run the planting, the irrigation and the harvest crews, which in summer is forty seasonal pickers plus our six regulars. I'm in the field at six, out of it when the light goes, and I'm on the phone to the supermarket's buyer in between about sizes and spec. I've never used AI and I don't want to; I write the crew rota on a whiteboard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you going in it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pride, mainly. My grandad grew leeks on this same soil before the farm was sold, and I'm the youngest field manager the owners have ever had. The pay's low for the hours, I've got about two weeks' money in the bank, and Tom and I are saving for our wedding next August. He's a mechanic in the village, and Sundays we're at chapel with his mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how it should be. Machines that help, not machines that take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always knew it was hype. Farming's about the soil and the weather and people who turn up, and no computer changes that. I'd say it at chapel and to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, though I'd still have the supermarkets squeezing us on price and rejecting carrots for being a bit bent. My worries are the buyers, the weather and the wedding money. AI was never on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep the crews tight, keep the buyer happy, and keep putting a little by for the wedding. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff even if it helped with paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like the field after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use it for paperwork if it's there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust what I don't understand. My mum always said, if you can't do it with a pencil, you don't really know it. Paperwork's slow, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the supermarket rejecting bent carrots. Who's to blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buyers, and the customers who only want perfect ones, honestly. It's a free market, so they can ask for what they want. But it breaks my heart seeing good carrots ploughed back in.

S0.say: I'd say I always knew it was hype, because farming is about soil, weather and people who turn up. No computer changes that.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but supermarkets would still squeeze us on price and reject carrots for being a bit bent. My worries are the buyers, the weather and the wedding money.
S0.do: Carries on running the crews and keeping the supermarket buyer happy. Keeps saving for her wedding and refuses to use AI tools even for paperwork.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like a field after rain.
S0.quote: If you can't do it with a pencil, you don't really know it.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is proud, rooted and openly distrustful of technology, and her mother's saying about the pencil sums up her stance. She accepts the free market's demands but grieves over waste. Faith, family and her coming wedding are at the centre of her life. She was calm and clear, with no gap between public and private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what they keep promising. Robot pickers. We'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines can't replace good people, and we'll still need crews who know a field. I'd tell the owners that I'll keep things running the way I know works. I'd say it plainly and not apologise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry. If the supermarkets push the farm to use robot harvesters to cut costs, the owners might listen, and then my crews shrink and maybe my job too. I'd be stuck between doing it the way I know and doing what the market wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd wait and see what the owners decide. I'd keep my crews loyal and do the best work I can so they don't want to replace me. I'd tighten our spending a bit and maybe push the wedding to a smaller do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a forecast that keeps changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our regulars, especially Mihai and his wife, who've come every season for eight years. They send money home to their kids. If a robot picks leeks, they've got nothing here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the owners asked you to run the robots, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes because I'd have to, but I'd be slow at it and I'd hate it. I'd rather they asked Tom, he likes anything with a motor. Maybe that's a thought, actually.

S1.say: I'd say machines can't replace good people and we'll still need crews who know a field. I'd tell the owners plainly that I'll keep running things the way I know works.
S1.think: I'd worry that supermarkets push the farm towards robot harvesters, shrinking my crews and maybe my job. I'd be stuck between my way and what the market wants.
S1.do: Waits to see what the owners decide while keeping her crews loyal and working hard so she isn't replaced. Tightens spending and considers a smaller wedding.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a forecast that keeps changing.
S1.quote: If a robot picks leeks, they've got nothing here.
S1.fieldNote: Uma's first worry was for a seasonal couple who've come for eight years, and her loyalty to her crew is strong. She would accept robots only grudgingly and would rather hand the job to her fiancé. Her free-market beliefs sit uneasily with the pressure from supermarkets. Waiting and hard work are her main strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord help us. That's barely two seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and it's not the way things should be done. People need work for their dignity, not just money. I'd say it at chapel and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished at Marsh End. If a robot can drill, weed, pick and grade, the owners don't need me or the crews, and the supermarket would be thrilled. I'd have nothing saved but the wedding money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the wedding money towards rent and bills straight away, and we'd marry at chapel with tea and cake in the hall instead. Tom and I would move in with his mum if we had to. I'd look for any work, cleaning, care homes, whatever's going, and lean on church and family before any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Heartbroken, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change for you, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no time to do anything but survive. With more time, I'd at least try something, maybe even learn the robots, like I said with the slower one. With two years, I'd just hold on to Tom and the chapel and get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said church and family before government. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how it's always worked for us. When my dad was out of work, the chapel brought meals for six months. I'd take help from people who know me before I'd take it from a form.

S2.say: I'd say this is wrong and not how things should be done, because people need work for their dignity, not just money. I'd say it at chapel and to anyone who'd listen.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished, because a robot that can drill, weed, pick and grade replaces me and the crews. I'd have nothing saved but the wedding money.
S2.do: Spends the wedding savings on rent and bills and marries at chapel with tea and cake instead. Moves in with her fiancé's mother if needed, takes any work going and leans on church and family before government schemes.
S2.quote: I'd take help from people who know me before I'd take it from a form.
S2.fieldNote: The wedding money became the emergency fund almost instantly, which said a lot about her priorities and her thin cushion. Her traditional outlook comes through in relying on chapel and family, drawn from real memory of her father's unemployment. She frames the loss in terms of dignity more than income. She didn't blame any single group, only said it was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but it gives you a bit of breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still wrong, but we'd have to get on with it. Farms should keep good people on as long as they can. And families and churches will need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job somewhere around the third year. I'd have a little time to save and maybe find something steady, but I don't know what. I've only ever done fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, we'd keep the wedding small and put the rest into savings, maybe two months' worth by the end. I'd keep doing my job well and see what the owners do. Maybe I'd ask about care work or the village school's kitchen, because people will still want someone real looking after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worried, but I'd still be sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI now. With five years, would you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. It's not who I am. Tom might, and I'd support him, but I'd rather do something with people than with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, at the end-of-season meal, that this might be the last few years. And I'd say make sure your families are close. That's what will get us through.

S3.say: I'd say it's still wrong but we'd have to get on with it. Farms should keep good people on as long as they can, and families and churches should look after each other.
S3.think: I think I'd lose my job around the third year, with a little time to save and find something steady. I've only ever done fields, so I don't know what.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding small and saves the rest, aiming for two months' money in the first year. Keeps working hard while watching the owners and asks about care work or the village school kitchen.
S3.feel: Anxious and worried, but still sleeping.
S3.quote: I'd rather do something with people than with screens.
S3.fieldNote: Even with five years, Uma would not learn AI and said so plainly; she would move towards care or kitchen work with people. She is honest about her limits. Her message to the crew, keep families close, fits her values. She sees her fiancé as the one who might adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that it doesn't feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people shouldn't panic. Good farmers will find a way. Families should prepare, but calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably not do much for the first few years. Ten years feels like forever when you're busy in the field. I'd hope it wouldn't really happen, and maybe it wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, nothing much: the wedding, the job, saving a bit. Around year five, if I saw robots on other farms, I'd look at care work or training as a teaching assistant. Tom and I might put off having children until we knew what work was left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little worry at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off children. Is that a big thing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I always wanted a family young, like my mum. But I wouldn't bring a baby into a house where nobody knew if there'd be work next year. That's the bit of this that would really hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope stays the same, even with robots in the fields?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sundays. Chapel, a roast, the whole family round the table. Robots can have the leeks if they must, but they can't have that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and people shouldn't panic, because good farmers will find a way. Families should prepare calmly.
S4.think: I think I'd do little for the first few years, because ten years feels like forever in the field. I'd hope it wouldn't really happen, and maybe it wouldn't.
S4.do: Carries on with the wedding, the job and modest saving in year one. Looks at care work or teaching-assistant training around year five if robots appear on other farms, and delays having children until work is clearer.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Robots can have the leeks if they must, but they can't have that.
S4.fieldNote: The longest warning time makes Uma less, not more, likely to act early. The real cost she named was delaying children, which clearly hurt to say. Her anchor is Sunday family life and chapel. She keeps her distance from technology in every scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose my job, the crew would lose theirs, and our wedding money would go on rent. What would help is farms keeping people on as long as they can, and churches and families being ready to look after each other. Maybe some help with training in care work, if it came through the college and not some faceless scheme.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the food. If robots grow it and supermarkets sell it, who still knows how to grow a leek? I'd want my children, if I have them, to know how.

headlineQuote: Robots can have the leeks if they must, but they can't have that.
portrait: Uma Ziegler is 27 and field manager on a 250-hectare vegetable farm supplying supermarkets, leading forty seasonal pickers with a whiteboard rota. She has about two weeks of savings and is saving for her wedding to Tom, a village mechanic. She never uses AI, trusts what she can do with a pencil, and leans on chapel and family rather than government. In the slower scenarios she waits and works hard; in the two-year picture she spends the wedding money on rent and turns to her church and family. With ten years she expects to do little at first, but would delay having children until work was clear.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her crew would lose their jobs and the wedding savings would go on rent.
whatWouldHelp: Farms keeping people on as long as possible, churches and families supporting each other, and care-work training through a local college.
